Rotator cuff tear arthropathy (CTA) is the final stage of the shoulder impingement syndrome
spectrum. It affects patients who have chronic, irreparable, massive rotator cuff tears (RCTs)
with superior migration of the humeral head, subchondral humeral head osteoporosis,
humeral head collapse, and painful debilitating shoulder arthritis.
Epidemiology
Affects women (3:1 female to male ratio), affects patients older than 70 years, and more
commonly affects the dominant shoulder

Epidemiology
Originally described as a clinical condition in the 19th century, the phrase “cuff tear
arthropathy” was not described until the 1980s, at which time Neer et al1 published a
series on 26 patients who underwent total shoulder arthroplasty. The condition was first
known as Milwaukee shoulder and was initially described in four elderly women with a
massive RCT and destructive arthritis.2 Further characteristics have been compiled,
demonstrating that CTA typically affects the dominant extremity of females older than
60 years.3 The condition has multiple proposed mechanisms but is thought to begin with
a disruption of dynamic stabilization provided by the rotator cuff, resulting in superior
migration of the humeral head and subsequent degenerative changes. However, CTA
only occurs in 4% of patients with a massive RCT.1 Additional studies are necessary to
better elucidate the causes and natural history of CTA.
Anatomy and Biomechanics
The glenohumeral joint is a complex joint regulated by an interaction between dynamic and
static forces that create a stable range of motion and fulcrum despite limited bony constraint.
The rotator cuff provides active stabilization of the glenohumeral joint by compressing the
humeral head against the glenoid, thereby providing a stable fulcrum for the deltoid to move
the shoulder.
Alterations in rotator cuff mechanics because of a massive tear or a disruption of the force
couple leads to a loss of stable humeral head compression, leading to superior migration

driven by the deltoid.
The humeral head abuts against the acromion, leading to additional disruption of normal
mechanics, and, over time, results in degenerative changes culminating in CTA.

Anatomy and Biomechanics
The rotator cuff is comprised of the supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, and
subscapularis. Each of these muscles are carefully balanced in force couples, with the
coronal plane balanced by the subscapularis, infraspinatus, and teres minor, and the
sagittal plane balanced by the supraspinatus and deltoid.4,5 In concert, these muscles
actively stabilize the glenohumeral joint by compressing the humeral head against the
glenoid. This action is most important in mid- and end-range motion.6 If these
compressive forces are disrupted, greater force is require to maintain a stable joint while
abducting the shoulder.7 Compensation can be provided by the latissimus dorsi and the
pectoralis major in patients with rotator cuff disruption; however, over time, the deltoid
becomes a primary deforming force, pulling the humeral head superiorly, allowing
impingement against the acromion.7,8 This migration has been demonstrated in vivo and
in multiple cadaver models.9-12 These altered mechanics subsequently diminish overall
shoulder function and cause progressive degenerative changes, resulting in CTA.
Etiology
Pathogenesis
Neer et al1 suggested mechanical, nutritional, and crystal-induced arthropathy pathways
(Figure 1); however, no definitive pathogenesis has been identified.

Figure 1
Diagram shows the nutritional and mechanical pathways involved in rotator cuff tear
arthropathy (CTA). A, Nutritional factors include the loss of a so-called watertight joint space
and a reduction in the pressure of the joint fluid that is required for the perfusion of
nutrients to the articular cartilage. Both contribute to the atrophy of cartilage and disuse
osteoporosis in the subchondral bone of the humeral head. B, Mechanical factors include
upward, anterior, and posterior instability of the humeral head. Upward instability escalates
wear into the anterior part of the acromion, the acromioclavicular (AC) joint, and the
coracoid. (Adapted with permission from Neer CS II, Craig EV, Fukuda H: Cuff-tear
arthropathy. J Bone Joint Surg Am 1983;65[9]:1232-1244.)

Mechanical factors: insufficient rotator cuff, superior migration of the humeral head,
instability, eccentric wear of the glenoid, humeral head deformity, and decreased shoulder
function
Nutritional: hypomobility-induced cartilage atrophy, poor nutrition (decrease in
glycosaminoglycans), dehydration, and subchondral osteoporosis
Crystalline-induced arthropathy: synovial-based matrix protein degradation destroys rotator
cuff tendons and cartilage; end-stage calcium-phosphate crystal deposition

Etiology
The pathogenesis of CTA is multifactorial and currently is incompletely understood.
Intrinsic and extrinsic causes are thought to be contributing factors. Intrinsic causes
include age-related degeneration of the rotator cuff tendons, tendon vascular supply
and anatomy, regional variation in tendon material properties, and structural
abnormalities in collagen fibers. Extrinsic causes are thought to be variations in
coracoacromial arch anatomy, tensile overload of the rotator cuff tendons, and
repetitive-use phenonema.13,14 The clinical condition of CTA was originally referred to as
Milwaukee shoulder, and was described in a series of four elderly women with bilateral
massive RCTs, destructive glenohumeral arthritis, and recurrent effusion. At the time,
Garancis et al2 noted an association between calcium phosphate crystals and arthritis.
This proposed mechanism has been further explored. After a massive RCT,
hydroxyapatite crystals slowly accumulate in the joint capsule, synovium, and cartilage.
Because of altered shoulder mechanics, these crystals are then released into synovial
fluid and subsequently phagocytosed by local cells, leading to a release of proteolytic
enzymes.2,15 Over time, these enzymes cause additional rotator cuff deterioration,
tissue destruction, and subsequent destructive arthritis.
Neer et al1 further explored this syndrome and termed the condition “rotator cuff tear
arthropathy”. The authors proposed a different mechanism, which included mechanical
and nutritional causes. In this theory, a massive RCT and rupture of the long head of the
biceps lead to superior migration of the humeral head and acromial impingement,
causing additional disruption of the rotator cuff. The loss of stabilization provided by the

rotator cuff leads to repetitive trauma to the joint surface, resulting in cartilage loss. This
cartilage loss is further compounded by a poor diffusion of nutrients through the
synovial fluid because of the loss of an enclosed joint space from the RCT. As mechanics
break down, shoulder range of motion and function are lost, leading to subchondral
osteopenia and humeral head erosions, which cause additional joint instability and
subsequent end-stage arthritis.1 This pathogenesis has been further explored in rat
models. RCTs were simulated by transecting or denervating the rotator cuff musculature
in rats, and glenohumeral cartilage was subsequently histologically examined at various
time intervals.16 In early stages, chondral cellular proliferation and a decrease in
proportion of trabecular bone were observed. Over time, the articular surface
experienced pitting and thinning, with a loss of cellular organization and a slow
replacement of subchondral bone with marrow.16 Another study using the same model
showed that loss of cartilage thickness occurred as early as 12 weeks, suggesting that
pathologic changes begin early in the process of altered joint mechanics.17
Another theory was proposed by Collins and Harryman.18 In this theory, the pathology
begins with a chronic degenerative tear in the supraspinatus. Over time, as the tear
enlarges, superior migration of the humeral head occurs, with impingement of the
remaining rotator cuff against the acromion. The pressure from impingement results in
humeral head wear, producing cartilage fragmentation and particulate wear. This debris
results in synovial thickening and effusion with generation of crystals. These crystals
then produce additional damage and debris via the action of proteolytic enzymes,
eventually resulting in end-stage arthritis.
Despite these proposed mechanisms, CTA occurs in only a small percentage of patients
with a massive RCT.1 Additional studies are necessary to understand the pathogenesis of
CTA, with a potential greater focus on cellular or genetic mechanisms in the future.
Natural History
Little data are available on the natural history of massive RCTs and CTA.
Neer et al1 estimated that CTA will occur in 4% of patients with a massive RCT.

Tear size, location, and chronicity can predict tear progression and humeral migration, with
tear size being most predictive.
Radiographic progression of arthritis may not necessarily correlate with symptoms or function.

Natural History
Currently, limited data are available on the natural history of massive RCTs and CTA
because massive RCTs are uncommonly managed nonsurgically and followed for the
long term. Small case series provide some understanding of the natural progression of
CTA. In a series of 19 patients with massive a RCT who were followed for 4 years, Zingg et
al19 showed a progression of glenohumeral arthritis, humeral head migration, increased
tear size, and increased fatty infiltration into rotator cuff tissue; however, patients
reported satisfactory functional outcomes at follow-up. Chalmers et al20 followed a
series of patients for 8 years. During that time, the authors documented radiographic
progression of arthritis in various RCT types and sizes; however, these changes were
small and did not appear to correlate with tear size. Other studies have documented
similar radiographic progression of migration over time; however, these findings have
not necessarily been correlated with symptoms or overall functional status.
Risk Factors
Risk factors: chronic RCT, hemorrhagic shoulder (oral anticoagulants and hematologic
diseases), rheumatic disease, and crystal-induced arthropathy
Classification
Hamada classification of RCA (Figure 2)


Classification
Several classification systems for RCA have been developed. The Hamada classification
system was originally described in 1990 to help classify massive RCTs on radiographs.21
This classification system measures changes in the acromiohumeral interval and bony
changes in the glenohumeral joint and the acromion. Grade 1 refers to an
acromiohumeral interval greater than 6 mm, and grade 2 refers to an acromiohumeral
interval of less than 5 mm measured on AP radiographs. Grade 3 refers to
acetabularization of the acromion, which, in the original description, may be result from
excavation of the acromion or excessive lateral spurring. Grade 4 is defined as grade 3
changes with narrowing of the glenohumeral joint. Grade 5 is the final stage and occurs
if the already mentioned findings are associated with humeral head collapse and is
considered to be CTA.22 Subsequent studies have shown the Hamada classification
system to have an intraobserver reliability ranging from 0.72 to 1.0 and an interobserver
reliability of 0.429.23 The Hamada classification system was further augmented by the
Seebauer classification system, which describes four subtypes quantified by the degree
of superior migration and instability of the joint. This allows the surgeon to account for
anterosuperior escape, which is associated with important clinical implications.24
Although reliable, the Hamada classification system does not provide any information on
the morphology of the glenoid, which may have important implications for surgical
management. This is better defined by the Favard classification system, which reports
four types of glenoid erosion. Type E0 is proximal migration without glenoid erosion,
type E1 refers to concentric erosion, type E2 refers to superior erosion, and type E3
refers to erosion extending inferiorly.25 The Favard classification system was expanded
to describe scapular notching after RSA.
The above classification systems were examined to determine their reliability among
observers and compared with other classification systems. Overall, the Sirveaux
classification system was found to be most reliable. The Hamada and Seebauer
classification systems showed reliability similar to that of the Kellgren-Lawrence scale,
which is commonly used for other forms of arthritis.26 Therefore, these classification

Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Chronic shoulder pain, night pain, weakness, and stiffness
Physical Examination
Inspection: supraspinatus and infraspinatus atrophy, anterior prominence of humeral head
with arm elevation (anterosuperior escape), and subcutaneous effusion (geyser sign)
Range of motion
Subacromial/glenohumeral crepitus with movement
Very limited range of motion for elevation, external rotator, and internal rotation
Pseudoparalysis: less than 90o elevation, lack of active external rotation, and incompetent
subscapularis
Chronic long head of the biceps rupture usually is present.
External rotation lag sign and hornblower sign (inability to maintain external rotation if the
shoulder is flexed 90° and abducted 90°, indicating teres minor insufficiency)
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Radiographs: AP, axillary, true AP
Acetabularization of the acromion and femoralization of the humeral head
Eccentric superior glenoid wear
Absence of typical peripheral osteophytes around the humeral head as observed in patients
with osteoarthritis
Osteopenia and subarticular sclerosis (snowcap sign)
Loss of the coracoacromial arch, indicating anterosuperior escape
Computed Tomography

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Not routinely necessary, especially if radiographs demonstrate anterosuperior escape
Establishes the extent of RCT, retraction, and fatty infiltration.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Indications
Patients with suitable range of motion for activities of daily living, manageable pain with
analgesic agents/injections, or patients unfit for surgical treatment
Techniques/Procedures
Rest, ice, NSAIDs, activity modifications, physical therapy, subacromial corticosteroid injection,
therapeutic ultrasonography, and laser therapy
If elevation is greater than 90°, then deltoid-strengthening exercises may improve function
and pain relief.
Pseudoparalytic shoulders usually do not improve with nonsurgical management.
Surgical Management
Indications
Failed nonsurgical management, pseudoparalytic shoulder, and uncontrolled pain with
nonsurgical management
Contraindications
Deltoid dysfunction, patients noncompliant with postoperative rehabilitation, chronic
infection, and poor glenohumeral bone stock

Techniques/Procedures
Surgical Approaches
Surgical procedures
Arthroscopic débridement
Unpredictable outcomes
Indication: pain relief in patients with full range of motion
Must preserve the coracoacromial arch (no coracoacromial ligament release or
acromioplasty) to avoid anterosuperior escape
Greater tuberosity tuberoplasty creates a smooth tuberosity-acromion interface.
Can be combined with adjuvant procedures, such as long head of the biceps tenotomy or
tenodesis and suprascapular nerve decompression
Hemiarthroplasty (humeral head replacement only)
Must have a functioning deltoid and preserved coracoacromial arch
Indicated in young, active patients
The combination of concentric glenoid reaming and a humeral head component (CTA
design) under the coracoacromial arch grant stability to the prosthesis.
Outcomes are limited; pain relief only; functional improvement of more than 90° of
elevation cannot be promised.
RSA (Figure 5)
Indications: pseudoparalytic shoulder, anterosuperior escape (insufficient coracoacromial
arch), age older than 70 years (controversial)
Functioning deltoid and adequate glenoid bone stock are mandatory.
Grammont design prosthesis moves the center of rotation inferiorly and medially to assist
the deltoid fulcrum and improve active abduction.
Outcomes are good and reproducible, especially pain relief (greater than 30% improvement
in Constant-Murley shoulder outcome score) and improved elevation (more than 100°);
external or internal rotation may not improve because of infraspinatus/teres minor and
subscapularis deficiency.
Good outcomes have extended the use of RSA to younger patients (>60 years).

Total shoulder arthroplasty and resurfacing prostheses are absolutely contraindicated in
patients with CTA; they lead to early glenoid loosening via the rocking horse phenomenon
and poor outcomes.
Postoperative Management
RSA rehabilitation
Sling is worn for 3 to 6 weeks postoperatively, followed by gradual active and active-assisted
range of motion in all planes.
Deltoid strengthening from supine to sitting is instituted at 6 to 8 weeks postoperatively.
Many patients are instructed to perform a home exercise program and do not require formal
physical therapy.
Pitfalls and Preventative Measures
Nonsurgical management should be maximized via physical therapy and NSAIDs.
Anterosuperior escape is an iatrogenic complication secondary to loss of the coracoacromial
arch after aggressive acromioplasty in combination with rotator cuff insufficiency. To avoid
anterosuperior escape, the coracoacromial arch should be preserved via arthroscopic
débridement and arthroplasty.
Glenoid implantation, which leads to early glenoid failure, should be avoided.
Anterior deltoid strengthening may provide good function in elderly patients with a massive
RCT.
Complications
Prosthetic replacement (RSA and hemiarthroplasty): infection, perioperative hematoma,
anterosuperior escape (hemiarthroplasty), instability, component wear, scapular notching,
acromion stress fractures, and residual pain and dysfunction
RSA is associated with a relatively higher complication rate compared with hemiarthroplasty.
Scapular notching
Increased frequency in traditional Grammont-style RSA implants (neckless component
design)
Incidence: 44% to 96%; however, the clinical relevance is controversial in the literature.
The medial and inferior center of rotation predispose patients to abutment of the humeral
component with the inferior scapular neck.
